lessons.name: Actuator sizing: torque, inertia and thermal duty
lessons.summary: Actuator sizing checks whether a motor and transmission can move a load at the required speed, repeatedly, without exceeding their limits.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Actuator sizing checks whether a motor and transmission can move a load at the required speed, repeatedly, without exceeding their limits.

![A force gauge pulls at a measured radius to determine shaft torque](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-sizing.webp)
*Measure force and lever arm to estimate starting torque. Source: [Oriental Motor](https://www.orientalmotor.com/technology/motor-sizing-calculations.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A moving arm needs more than holding torque:** acceleration adds demand beyond gravity and friction.
- **Repeated demonstrations are a workload:** size for the complete motion pattern, not just the most impressive movement.
- **A catalogue value has conditions:** maxon explains that temperature, installation and control settings affect motor behaviour.

> **Key idea:** Treat the full motion cycle as the specification, not a single torque number.

## How it works

- **Start at the load:** list masses, dimensions, friction, movement time and speed before picking a motor.
- **Think of server capacity planning:** one successful request does not prove sustained throughput; one successful lift does not prove repeated operation.
- **Calculate twisting demand:** force acting perpendicular to a lever produces torque; add the torque needed to accelerate the rotating parts.
- **Account for gearing:** reduction trades speed for torque, but the motor's spinning rotor also contributes inertia at the joint.
- **Check heat separately:** effective load torque weights the changing torque demand across the cycle; compare it with continuous-operation limits, not just peak capability.
- **Read the conditions:** a warm motor differs from a cold motor; simulation does not replace physical testing.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  L["Load and motion"] --> T["Torque and speed"]
  T --> G["Motor and gearing"]
  G --> C["Cycle and heat checks"]
  C --> V["Physical validation"]
```

## Key terms

- **Torque**: twisting effort, measured in newton-metres.
- **Inertia**: resistance to changing rotational speed; it exists even when the object is stationary.
- **Duty cycle**: the pattern of movement, holding and rest over time.
- **Continuous rating**: an operating limit intended for sustained operation under stated conditions.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Read Electric actuator architectures: mechanical trade-offs and separate motor-side quantities from joint-side quantities.
- **After:** Build Torque-speed envelope from a load case, then Joint duty-cycle thermal estimator before considering hardware.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Create a hypothetical load:** a perpendicular 10 N force at 0.10 m needs 1 N·m of holding torque, using Oriental Motor's force-times-radius relation.
2. **Add movement phases:** label acceleration, constant speed, deceleration and holding; identify where extra acceleration torque appears.
3. **Compare repeated cycles:** use the effective-torque method in the sizing reference, keeping all units consistent.
4. **Reject missing inputs:** if thermal or continuous-rating data are absent, mark sustained operation unknown rather than accepting a peak number.

lessons.name: Backdrivability, friction and mechanical transparency
lessons.summary: Backdrivability lets a load turn a motor through its transmission; mechanical transparency means feeling little added resistance from the mechanism.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Backdrivability lets a load turn a motor through its transmission; mechanical transparency means feeling little added resistance from the mechanism.

![ODRI actuator module with motor, belts and output pulley visible](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-backdrivability.webp)
*ODRI's documented actuator uses two belt-reduction stages. Source: [ODRI actuator documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-dynamic-robot-initiative/open_robot_actuator_hardware/master/mechanics/actuator_module_v1/README.md), BSD 3-Clause License.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Contact runs both ways:** the motor pushes the world, but the world can also push the robot.
- **A heavy-feeling joint hides interaction:** the person or environment must accelerate the mechanism as well as the robot link.
- **Legged robots need this distinction:** MIT Cheetah research explicitly connects backdrivability with impact mitigation.

> **Key idea:** Torque amplification also amplifies the rotor inertia felt from the output side.

## How it works

- **Follow the reverse path:** turning the output makes the motor rotor spin through the transmission, if the mechanism permits it.
- **Use a middleware analogy:** the payload is the intended interaction; friction and added inertia are overhead between the user and that interaction.
- **Separate two obstacles:** friction resists motion, while inertia resists changes in speed; reducing one does not erase the other.
- **Square the reduction:** Modern Robotics gives apparent rotor inertia as gear ratio squared times rotor inertia, measured at the joint.
- **Work the comparison:** increasing reduction from 10 to 100 multiplies this rotor contribution by 100, for the same motor; it does not merely multiply it by ten.
- **Look at real hardware:** ODRI documents two 3:1 belt stages giving 9:1 overall reduction; the architecture paper evaluates the resulting interaction behaviour.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["External push"] --> O["Joint output"]
  O --> T["Transmission"]
  T --> R["Motor rotor"]
  R --> F["Added inertia and friction"]
```

## Key terms

- **Backdrivability**: ability to move the actuator from its output side.
- **Transparency**: how little the mechanism's own resistance obscures the intended mechanical interaction.
- **Reflected inertia**: inertia expressed as it is felt through a transmission at another shaft.
- **Friction**: resistance that dissipates mechanical energy; bearings and transmission contacts contribute.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Read Actuator sizing: torque, inertia and thermal duty and Spur and planetary gear trains.
- **After:** Try Reflected inertia gear-ratio dashboard before Low-impedance joint architecture comparison.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Normalize rotor inertia:** set it to one arbitrary unit and calculate the apparent contribution for reductions 10 and 100.
2. **Plot the results:** obtain 100 and 10,000 units respectively; label these model values, not measurements of a real actuator.
3. **Add a friction slider:** compare zero friction with nonzero resistance, keeping rotor inertia unchanged.
4. **Explain the limits:** the plot predicts a trend, not the friction or contact safety of an actual robot.

lessons.name: Spur and planetary gear trains
lessons.summary: Gear trains use meshing teeth to exchange speed for torque; planetary trains arrange moving planet gears around a central sun gear.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Gear trains use meshing teeth to exchange speed for torque; planetary trains arrange moving planet gears around a central sun gear.

![Labelled planetary gear showing sun, planet gears, carrier and ring gear](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-gears.webp)
*Identify which part is fixed before calculating a ratio. Source: [tec-science](https://www.tec-science.com/mechanical-power-transmission/planetary-gear/epicyclic-planetary-gear/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Motors and joints want different motion:** a gear reduction slows the output while increasing available torque.
- **Packaging changes the design:** planetary arrangements can keep input and output on the same axis.
- **A teaching model answers limited questions:** counting rotations explains reduction; it does not establish a gearbox's load capacity.

> **Key idea:** Tooth counts alone are not enough for a planetary ratio; identify the fixed part, input and output.

## How it works

- **Start with two spur gears:** these toothed wheels mesh directly; external gears rotate in opposite directions.
- **Count teeth passing contact:** Woodgears' 7-tooth driver turns three times for one turn of its 21-tooth partner.
- **Think of composed functions:** successive reduction stages multiply their ratios, just as composed scaling functions multiply their scale factors.
- **Recognize the planetary parts:** a sun sits centrally, planets turn around it, a carrier supports their shafts, and an internally toothed ring surrounds them.
- **Choose the constraint:** fixing the ring while driving the sun makes the carrier the slower output; fixing another part changes the result.
- **Work a published example:** tec-science uses a 12-tooth sun, 18-tooth planets and 48-tooth ring; fixed-ring operation gives five sun turns per carrier turn.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["Sun input"] --> P["Meshing planets"]
  R["Fixed ring"] --> P
  P --> C["Carrier output"]
```

## Key terms

- **Reduction ratio**: input turns divided by output turns; state this convention because some references use its reciprocal.
- **Carrier**: the moving support for planet shafts, not another toothed wheel.
- **Pitch**: tooth spacing; meshing gears need compatible tooth spacing.
- **Backlash**: clearance that allows some motion on reversal before the opposite tooth surfaces engage.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Review Electric actuator architectures: mechanical trade-offs and basic ratios.
- **After:** Build Planetary tooth-count explorer, then Hand-cranked printed planetary cutaway using FreeCAD.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Sketch the published set:** label sun 12, planet 18 and ring 48; check that sun plus twice planet equals ring.
2. **Fix the ring:** animate five sun rotations and predict one carrier rotation in the same direction.
3. **Change the fixed member:** fix the carrier instead and compare the ring's direction and turn count with tec-science's table.
4. **Document the boundary:** report the kinematic ratio, leaving strength, friction and backlash unknown until separately evaluated.

lessons.name: Cycloidal reducers and output mechanisms
lessons.summary: A cycloidal reducer turns an eccentric input into slow output rotation using a lobed disc, a ring of pins and an output mechanism.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

A cycloidal reducer turns an eccentric input into slow output rotation using a lobed disc, a ring of pins and an output mechanism.

![Exploded cycloidal reducer with eccentric input, fixed pins, lobed disc and output pin disc](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-cycloidal.webp)
*The output pins pass through holes in the moving disc. Source: [tec-science](https://www.tec-science.com/mechanical-power-transmission/planetary-gear/how-does-a-cycloidal-gear-drive-work/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Follow the complete transmission:** watching the disc wobble is not enough; a robot joint needs rotation about a supported output axis.
- **Ratio is only one requirement:** the disc profile, eccentric motion and output clearances must also fit together.
- **Commercial designs add structure:** Nabtesco's RV mechanism combines two reduction stages, balancing and support bearings rather than relying on a single printed disc.

> **Key idea:** The output mechanism must transmit the disc's slow rotation without copying its sideways wobble.

## How it works

- **Start off-centre:** the input shaft carries an eccentric, whose rotation moves the disc's centre around a small circle.
- **Constrain the disc:** its lobes engage fixed surrounding pins, so it slowly rotates while its centre orbits.
- **Extract useful rotation:** rollers on an output pin disc engage the moving disc's holes; the output shaft stays on the gearbox's central axis.
- **Think of an adapter function:** the disc produces combined orbit and rotation; the output mechanism exposes only the rotation your joint needs.
- **Count a published example:** tec-science uses 10 fixed pins and nine disc lobes; nine input turns produce one output turn in the opposite direction.
- **Balance matters:** two discs offset by 180° can counter unbalanced forces; Nabtesco also uses two RV gears to balance forces.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["Input rotation"] --> E["Eccentric motion"]
  E --> D["Orbiting lobed disc"]
  P["Fixed pins"] --> D
  D --> O["Output rollers"]
  O --> S["Slow output shaft"]
```

## Key terms

- **Eccentric**: a rotating feature whose centre is offset from the main shaft axis.
- **Lobe**: a rounded protrusion on the disc's working profile.
- **Output pin disc**: a plate carrying pins or rollers that collect the disc's rotation.
- **Clearance**: space between mating parts that permits motion; it is not a substitute for a specified profile.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Inspect Nabtesco RV reducer family and use FreeCAD to identify input, fixed housing and output parts.
- **After:** Start Cycloidal eccentric-to-output animation, then Hand-driven cycloidal tolerance experiment before Guarded dual-disc cycloidal joint prototype.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Reproduce the 10-pin example:** label the nine-lobed disc, eccentric and output rollers in an offline animation.
2. **Track separate motions:** draw attention to the disc's moving centre and the output shaft's fixed centre.
3. **Count nine input turns:** verify one reversed output turn; compare against the published animation.
4. **Remove the output rollers virtually:** explain why the disc still moves but no longer drives that output shaft.

lessons.name: Strain-wave gearing and flexspline design
lessons.summary: Strain-wave gearing uses a rotating oval to flex a toothed sleeve against a rigid ring, creating a large reduction from a small tooth-count difference.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Strain-wave gearing uses a rotating oval to flex a toothed sleeve against a rigid ring, creating a large reduction from a small tooth-count difference.

![Separated wave generator, thin toothed flexspline cup and rigid circular spline](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-strain-wave.webp)
*The three parts have different mechanical jobs. Source: [Harmonic Drive](https://www.harmonicdrive.net/technology), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Compact reduction is attractive:** Harmonic Drive describes a three-element mechanism that puts a large reduction into a small package.
- **Flexing is deliberate:** the flexible metal part is not a broken rigid gear; its shape change is essential to operation.
- **Assembly affects performance:** the manufacturer specifies matched components, alignment tolerances and lubrication, not just tooth counts.

> **Key idea:** The flexspline must change shape radially while still transmitting torque to the output.

## How it works

- **Insert the wave generator:** its elliptical hub and flexible bearing force the thin flexspline into an oval.
- **Engage opposite regions:** external flexspline teeth mesh with the internally toothed circular spline near the oval's two ends.
- **Rotate the oval:** the engagement zones move around the ring; the flexspline has two fewer teeth, so it progressively turns relative to the ring.
- **Use a version-offset analogy:** two cyclic sequences almost align, but their small length difference creates a slowly shifting correspondence.
- **Work the manufacturer's example:** Nabtesco describes a 200-tooth flexspline and two-tooth difference giving 100:1 reduction with the circular spline fixed.
- **Check the direction:** each full clockwise wave-generator turn shifts the flexspline two teeth counterclockwise relative to the fixed ring.
- **Treat ratings as conditional:** Harmonic Drive's fatigue-life statement applies within catalogue ratings; it does not certify a different material or printed geometry.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["Rotating wave generator"] --> F["Flexspline becomes oval"]
  C["Fixed circular spline"] --> E["Two engagement zones"]
  F --> E
  E --> O["Slow flexspline output"]
```

## Key terms

- **Wave generator**: the elliptical input hub and bearing that create the travelling deformation.
- **Flexspline**: the thin, externally toothed flexible cup or sleeve.
- **Circular spline**: the rigid internally toothed ring.
- **Radial compliance**: ability to change shape across the radius.
- **Torsional stiffness**: resistance to twisting under torque; different from the absence of backlash.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Inspect Harmonic Drive strain-wave gearing and identify its three parts in FreeCAD or a published cutaway.
- **After:** Build Strain-wave tooth engagement explainer before Printed flexspline fit and compliance coupons.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Label the three components:** distinguish the bearing-containing input from the flexible toothed output.
2. **Track one input turn:** mark the two-tooth reverse shift with the circular spline fixed.
3. **Check the 200-tooth example:** divide 200 by two to recover 100 input turns per output turn.
4. **List design constraints:** record alignment, lubrication and matched-set requirements; leave any proposed printed part's load rating unknown.

lessons.name: Timing-belt and capstan transmissions
lessons.summary: Timing belts transmit motion through meshing teeth; capstans transmit pull through friction between a wrapped cable and a drum.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Timing belts transmit motion through meshing teeth; capstans transmit pull through friction between a wrapped cable and a drum.

![ODRI actuator opened to show two toothed belts, pulleys and the output shaft](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-belt-capstan.webp)
*A real two-stage timing-belt transmission, not a friction capstan. Source: [ODRI assembly guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-dynamic-robot-initiative/open_robot_actuator_hardware/master/mechanics/actuator_module_v1/details/details_actuator_module_assembly.md), BSD 3-Clause License.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Motor location is a design choice:** a belt can transmit motion while the heavy motor stays elsewhere on the structure.
- **Assembly sets behaviour:** MIT's design notes emphasize belt tension, secure clamps and pulley tracking, not merely a nominal reduction ratio.
- **Cable drives have travel limits:** a helical cable wrap moves along the capstan during actuation, unlike an endlessly circulating belt.

> **Key idea:** Teeth locate a timing belt; friction and maintained tension make a capstan transmit force.

## How it works

- **Follow the timing belt:** its teeth engage matching pulley teeth, carrying tension from the driving pulley to the driven pulley.
- **Follow the capstan cable:** wrapping increases frictional grip, but the cable still needs positive tension and properly secured ends.
- **Think of two API contracts:** a timing belt specifies geometric engagement; a capstan relies on a friction-and-tension condition that can fail through slipping.
- **Inspect a documented reduction:** ODRI uses two 3:1 stages; multiplying them gives 9:1 overall, so nine motor turns produce one output turn.
- **Separate the mechanisms:** that 9:1 belt example does not establish a capstan's load capacity; wrap, friction and preload require their own model.
- **Check reversal:** ODRI's assembly guide asks you to turn the output back and forth; MIT also highlights tensioner stiffness and alignment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M["Motor rotation"] --> B["Toothed belt and pulleys"]
  B --> O["Output motion"]
  M --> C["Wrapped cable and drum"]
  T["Positive cable tension"] --> C
  C --> O
```

## Key terms

- **Timing belt**: a flexible toothed belt that indexes motion through matching pulley teeth.
- **Capstan**: a drum that transmits cable force through wrapped contact and friction.
- **Preload**: tension applied before the working load, helping keep cable contact.
- **Tracking**: a belt's movement along the pulley axis.
- **Pitch**: distance between neighbouring belt teeth.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Inspect ODRI actuator module and locate its motor, intermediate pulley and output pulley.
- **After:** Use Belt and capstan preload explorer before Hand-driven belt tension reversal rig or Remote-drive elbow transmission fixture.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Trace the ODRI belt path:** label both 3:1 stages in the published assembly photographs.
2. **Calculate total reduction:** predict one output revolution for nine motor revolutions, ignoring elastic stretch.
3. **Compare a cable layout:** sketch its helical wrap and identify where cable travel would run out.
4. **Model loss of preload:** set slack-side tension to zero in a friction model; explain why adding wraps cannot restore the missing contact force.

lessons.name: Lead screws, ball screws and linear joint packaging
lessons.summary: A screw drive converts rotation into straight-line travel; its screw, nut, bearings and guides must work together as one linear joint.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

A screw drive converts rotation into straight-line travel; its screw, nut, bearings and guides must work together as one linear joint.

![Ball screw and nut beside a sliding lead screw with an anti-backlash nut](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-linear-screws.webp)
*Rolling and sliding screw drives package their nuts differently. Source: [MIT design notes](https://fab.cba.mit.edu/classes/865.24/topics/mechanical_design/mechanical_design/transmissions/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Linear motion needs more than a motor:** a nut moves along the screw while guides constrain the carriage's unwanted motion.
- **Contact changes the trade-off:** rolling balls reduce friction, but their recirculation mechanism makes the nut assembly bulkier.
- **Alignment is part of the design:** MIT notes that a screw alongside two linear rails creates multiple constraints that must agree.

> **Key idea:** Screw lead sets travel per turn; guide alignment determines whether the assembled axis can actually move freely.

## How it works

- **Rotate one part relative to the other:** the screw's helical thread advances the nut along its axis.
- **Choose sliding or rolling contact:** a lead screw slides against its nut; a ball screw circulates balls between matching grooves.
- **Think of a unit-conversion adapter:** the drive maps motor revolutions to carriage distance; the conversion factor is the screw's lead.
- **Work the igus example:** a single-start 20-threads-per-inch screw advances one twentieth of an inch per turn, or 0.05 inches.
- **Do not confuse lead and pitch:** they coincide for a single-start thread, but multiple thread starts increase travel per revolution.
- **Package the supports:** reserve space for the nut, end supports, motor connection and guides; a ball-return assembly is not an empty sleeve.
- **Inspect reversals:** sliding nuts need clearance to move; that clearance can appear as lost motion before reversed travel begins.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M["Motor turns"] --> S["Screw and nut"]
  S --> C["Carriage translation"]
  G["Aligned linear guides"] --> C
  C --> L["Load moves straight"]
```

> **Watch out:** Ball screws can backdrive under gravity; do not rely on an unassessed screw to retain a vertical load.

## Key terms

- **Lead**: distance advanced per relative revolution of screw and nut.
- **Pitch**: spacing between neighbouring threads.
- **Start**: one continuous helical thread running along a screw.
- **Backdriving**: an external linear load causing the screw mechanism to rotate.
- **Backlash**: clearance taken up after reversing direction before output movement resumes.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Use FreeCAD to distinguish the screw, nut, carriage and guide constraints in a linear-axis model.
- **After:** Build Screw lead force-speed visualizer, then Horizontal screw-guide alignment jig before Supported linear joint module.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Model the 20-TPI example:** display 0.05 inches of nut travel for each revolution.
2. **Command ten turns:** predict 0.50 inches of travel and label this ideal geometry, not positioning accuracy.
3. **Introduce virtual misalignment:** offset a guide relative to the screw and identify the conflicting constraints.
4. **Compare nut envelopes:** reserve different space for rolling-ball recirculation and a sliding nut; record unspecified dimensions as unknown.

lessons.name: Electric actuator architectures: mechanical trade-offs
lessons.summary: An electric actuator combines a motor with the transmission, bearings and structure needed to turn electrical effort into useful joint motion.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

An electric actuator combines a motor with the transmission, bearings and structure needed to turn electrical effort into useful joint motion.

![ODRI module subassemblies including motor rotor, stator, encoder, pulleys and bearing-equipped shells](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-electric-architectures.webp)
*The motor is only one part of the joint assembly. Source: [ODRI assembly guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-dynamic-robot-initiative/open_robot_actuator_hardware/master/mechanics/actuator_module_v1/details/details_actuator_module_assembly.md), BSD 3-Clause License.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A command protocol is not a mechanism:** choosing a motor family does not decide how its shaft supports or moves a robot link.
- **Packaging carries the load:** ODRI's assembly includes bearing-equipped shells, a motor, transmission and encoder.
- **Compare operating points:** motor torque and speed must suit the load through the selected transmission, not merely look impressive separately.

> **Key idea:** Choose the complete motor-to-load architecture, not a motor name or a single torque specification.

## How it works

- **Begin with the rotating parts:** a rotor turns relative to a stator; electromagnetic forces produce the motor's torque.
- **Compare brushed and brushless layouts:** brushed motors switch winding current mechanically through brushes; brushless motors require electronic switching.
- **Consider steppers separately:** successive electrical excitations move their rotor in discrete steps; available torque depends on speed and the driver.
- **Use a software dependency analogy:** selecting a motor is selecting a library, while the actuator also needs the adapter, runtime and interfaces that make it usable.
- **Add a transmission when needed:** gearing or belts exchange motor speed for joint torque; direct drive connects the load without a reduction stage.
- **Work a concrete stepper example:** Oriental Motor describes a 1.8° full step, giving 360 divided by 1.8, or 200 full steps per revolution.
- **Avoid a false guarantee:** counting commanded steps is not proof of achieved motion; the same reference explains loss of synchronism under unsuitable loads.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["Electrical drive"] --> M["Motor"]
  M --> T["Transmission or direct drive"]
  T --> J["Joint motion"]
  B["Bearings and housing"] --> J
  E["Encoder measurement"] --> D
  J --> E
```

## Key terms

- **Rotor**: the motor part that rotates.
- **Stator**: the motor part treated as stationary relative to its housing.
- **Transmission**: mechanism that transfers or transforms motor motion.
- **Encoder**: sensor measuring rotation.
- **Operating point**: the torque and speed requested together, rather than independent catalogue maxima.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Use FreeCAD to inspect a proposed joint's mounting faces, bearing locations and motor clearance.
- **After:** Start Motor architecture decision notebook, then Interchangeable motor mounting plate study before Modular rotary joint cartridge.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Make a comparison table:** list a brushed motor, brushless motor and stepper; separate motor properties from transmission and support choices.
2. **Reproduce the step count:** compute 200 full steps per revolution for the documented 1.8° example.
3. **Annotate ODRI's subassemblies:** trace how the motor, belts, bearings, shell and encoder connect.
4. **Record missing specifications:** leave mass, torque-speed limits and thermal data unknown unless a specific motor's documentation supplies them.

lessons.name: Linkages, cams and parallel mechanism design
lessons.summary: Linkages and cams turn a chosen input motion into a constrained output path, using connected bars or a shaped contact surface.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Linkages and cams turn a chosen input motion into a constrained output path, using connected bars or a shaped contact surface.

![Two branches of a planar parallel linkage meet at a shared endpoint in an Onshape assembly](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-linkages.webp)
*Two mechanical paths connect the base to the same moving point. Source: [onshape-to-robot](https://onshape-to-robot.readthedocs.io/en/latest/kinematic_loops.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Geometry can do work for your code:** connected bars can coordinate motion without a separate motor at every hinge.
- **Remote actuation changes packaging:** a parallelogram can transmit movement while keeping a motor away from the moving endpoint.
- **A valid pose is not every pose:** closed chains constrain which combinations of joint angles are physically possible.

> **Key idea:** A mechanism is a physical constraint solver; choose the permitted motion before choosing the motor.

## How it works

- **Picture a four-bar:** four rigid bars form a loop, including the fixed base; turning one bar determines the others' compatible positions.
- **Think of database constraints:** a closed loop must satisfy all connections simultaneously, just as related records must satisfy their shared keys.
- **Try a parallelogram:** in the ideal geometry, opposite bars stay parallel; the output bar follows the input bar's rotation.
- **Compare a cam:** a rotating shaped surface pushes a contacting follower, converting the profile into a prescribed movement.
- **Add parallel branches:** several chains meet at one platform; the chains must agree on the same endpoint position.
- **Export carefully:** onshape-to-robot breaks a closed chain into a tree, then adds constraints to reconnect it in supported simulation formats.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["Input rotation"] --> G["Bars or cam profile"]
  G --> C["Geometric constraints"]
  C --> P["Output path"]
```

## Key terms

- **Link**: one body treated as rigid when describing the mechanism.
- **Revolute joint**: a hinge allowing rotation about one axis.
- **Prismatic joint**: a connection allowing sliding along one axis.
- **Closed chain**: connected links that form a loop rather than a branching tree.
- **Follower**: the part whose motion is imposed by contact with a cam.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Know basic geometry; use CAD and design for manufacture of robot joints to distinguish a rigid part from an assembly connection.
- **After:** Explore Four-bar path sketchbook, then Cardboard cam and follower comparison and Parallel-link remote-actuated joint prototype.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Draw a hypothetical parallelogram:** use opposite lengths of 100 mm and 50 mm, with the 100 mm base fixed.
2. **Rotate the input in CAD:** record several compatible poses; compare the input and output bar orientations.
3. **Change one length:** replace one 50 mm bar with 60 mm; observe why the output no longer follows the same parallelogram rule.
4. **Watch the cam animation:** identify the driving bar, cam and follower, then describe which part encodes the output motion.

lessons.name: Tendon routing, antagonism and underactuated mechanisms
lessons.summary: Tendon mechanisms transmit pulling forces through cables, while routing, opposing springs and shared actuation determine how their joints move.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Tendon mechanisms transmit pulling forces through cables, while routing, opposing springs and shared actuation determine how their joints move.

![RUKA finger assembly showing linked printed finger segments and extension springs](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-tendons.webp)
*RUKA uses routed string and extension springs in its printed fingers. Source: [RUKA project](https://ruka-hand.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Motors need not sit in fingers:** tendons carry motion from a remote motor to lightweight moving links.
- **One motor can coordinate several joints:** this reduces independent commands but makes motion depend on mechanical coupling and contact.
- **Routing is part of the model:** RUKA documents tube placement and string routing, not just the hand's visible outer shape.

> **Key idea:** A motor command specifies tendon motion, not a guaranteed angle at every joint it crosses.

## How it works

- **Picture a string over a pulley:** shortening the string pulls a joint; a slack string cannot transmit a pushing force.
- **Provide the return path:** an extension spring can reopen a finger, or an opposing tendon can pull in the other direction.
- **Think of a shared event handler:** one input triggers several linked responses; you cannot set each response independently without changing the architecture.
- **Read a real assembly:** RUKA's finger instructions connect three printed joint parts with two dowels, then install two extension springs.
- **Track the route:** RUKA guides tendons through PTFE tubes, a plastic tubing material; its guide specifies their order through the wrist.
- **Distinguish mechanism and measurement:** RUKA has no joint encoders, meaning angle sensors; its project learns mappings from motor positions to joint or fingertip positions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M["Motor pulley"] --> T["Tendon route"]
  T --> J["Coupled joints"]
  J --> S["Return springs"]
  S --> T
```

## Key terms

- **Tendon**: a flexible cable or string transmitting tension, meaning pulling force.
- **Antagonism**: opposing pulls acting on the same mechanism.
- **Underactuation**: fewer independently controlled actuator inputs than mechanical degrees of freedom.
- **Slack**: loose tendon length that must be taken up before tension can move the joint.
- **Degree of freedom**: an independent coordinate describing possible motion.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Read Timing-belt and capstan transmissions and Linkages, cams and parallel mechanism design to understand pulleys and coupled movement.
- **After:** Start Tendon routing and slack simulator, then compare Antagonistic tendon hinge board with Underactuated tendon differential demonstrator.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Copy the documented finger layout:** sketch three joint parts, two connecting dowels and the two return springs; no powered hardware is needed.
2. **Trace each tendon:** mark every bend and guide from finger attachment to motor pulley; distinguish tendon length from joint angle.
3. **Model two hypothetical cases:** assign zero slack, then 5 mm slack; the first 5 mm of take-up produces no tension in the second model.
4. **Compare against RUKA's video:** explain why a learned motor-to-fingertip mapping is different from measuring every joint directly.

lessons.name: Series-elastic actuator mechanics
lessons.summary: A series-elastic actuator places a deliberate spring between the drive and the load, using spring deflection to estimate transmitted force or torque.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

A series-elastic actuator places a deliberate spring between the drive and the load, using spring deflection to estimate transmitted force or torque.

![MIT Cog diagram placing a spring between a geared motor and the actuator load](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-series-elastic.webp)
*The spring sits in the force-transmission path, not beside it. Source: [MIT Cog Project](http://www.ai.mit.edu/projects/cog/MotorSystem/actuators.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Contact changes the problem:** a motor that reaches an angle accurately does not automatically apply a gentle force to an object.
- **A spring makes load visible:** measuring how far it bends gives information about transmitted effort after the drive.
- **Compliance has a cost:** MIT's Cog documentation identifies reduced overall bandwidth, meaning limited ability to follow fast changes.

> **Key idea:** Measure both ends of the spring; motor motion alone is no longer the output motion.

## How it works

- **Picture motor, spring, then load:** the motor can move while the load stays still, compressing or twisting the spring between them.
- **Think of a bounded buffer:** input and output can temporarily differ; the spring stores mechanical energy rather than messages.
- **Calibrate the relationship:** for an ideal linear spring, doubling its displacement doubles the transmitted force.
- **Use a toy calculation:** a hypothetical 100 N/m spring compressed by 0.01 m transmits 1 N; these are exercise inputs, not a robot specification.
- **Close the force loop:** compare measured spring displacement with the displacement corresponding to the desired force, then adjust the drive.
- **Keep geometry in view:** a rotary spring relates twist to torque; a linear spring relates displacement to force, so their stiffness units differ.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["Drive"] --> S["Series spring"]
  S --> L["Load"]
  S --> E["Deflection measurement"]
  E --> C["Force controller"]
  C --> D
```

## Key terms

- **Compliance**: willingness to deform under an applied force or torque.
- **Stiffness**: change in force per displacement, or torque per angular displacement.
- **Deflection**: the spring's displacement from its unloaded configuration.
- **Bandwidth**: the range of changing commands an actuator can follow effectively.
- **Series**: arranged so transmitted effort passes through the spring on its way to the load.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Read Actuator sizing: torque, inertia and thermal duty and Backdrivability, friction and mechanical transparency; distinguish the motor from the joint output.
- **After:** Explore Spring-in-series resonance notebook and Passive series-spring calibration board before Guarded series-elastic rotary joint.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Create a spreadsheet:** enter the hypothetical 100 N/m stiffness and displacements of 0, 0.005 and 0.01 m.
2. **Calculate force:** obtain 0, 0.5 and 1 N; plot force against displacement to see the calibration slope.
3. **Separate drive and load:** draw their positions independently and label their difference as spring deflection.
4. **Inspect the real mechanism:** use IHMC's assembly animation to identify the motor, screw, carriage and spring-related measurement path.

lessons.name: Variable-stiffness and antagonistic spring mechanisms
lessons.summary: Variable-stiffness mechanisms physically adjust how strongly a joint resists displacement, using springs, shaped cams or opposing drives rather than only controller gains.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Variable-stiffness mechanisms physically adjust how strongly a joint resists displacement, using springs, shaped cams or opposing drives rather than only controller gains.

![DLR Floating Spring Joint diagram identifying its position motor, stiffness motor, cam disks and rollers](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-variable-stiffness.webp)
*DLR separates joint positioning from adjustment of the spring mechanism. Source: [DLR](https://www.dlr.de/en/rm/research/robotic-systems/humanoids/david/mechatronics-of-david), CC BY-NC-ND 3.0.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Position and softness are separate choices:** the same target angle can have different physical resistance to an unexpected push.
- **Energy can be stored deliberately:** DLR demonstrates a spring-assisted throwing motion, rather than treating all deformation as an error.
- **More adjustability needs more mechanism:** DLR uses different actuator arrangements in the hand, wrist and upper arm.

> **Key idea:** Check the passive force–displacement curve, not just the controller's requested stiffness value.

## How it works

- **Start with a series spring:** DLR's Floating Spring Joint places a nonlinear spring mechanism between its main gear and output.
- **Add a second adjustment:** a large motor sets joint position; a smaller motor changes the stiffness preset of a single spring mechanism.
- **Shape the conversion:** cams and rollers turn joint twist into compression of a linear spring; the cam profile changes the torque response.
- **Compare antagonism:** DLR's hand uses two equivalent motors and progressive tendon springs to adjust joint position and stiffness.
- **Think of changing buffer capacity:** altering physical storage changes what the system can absorb; changing a software gain changes its response policy instead.
- **Keep damping separate:** stiffness resists displacement; damping resists motion and removes energy, so an elastic joint can still need active vibration control.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Position motor"] --> O["Joint equilibrium"]
  S["Stiffness motor"] --> C["Cam and spring preset"]
  O --> F["Force versus deflection"]
  C --> F
```

## Key terms

- **Passive stiffness**: mechanical resistance produced by the mechanism itself, rather than feedback corrections alone.
- **Equilibrium**: the configuration where opposing effects balance.
- **Progressive spring**: a spring mechanism whose resistance increases more steeply as it deforms.
- **Cam**: a shaped contact surface that determines another part's movement.
- **Damping**: an effect that dissipates motion energy rather than storing and returning it.
- **Radian (rad)**: a unit measuring rotation; rotational stiffness describes torque change per radian.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Study Series-elastic actuator mechanics and Linkages, cams and parallel mechanism design to separate spring behaviour from geometric conversion.
- **After:** Inspect DLR David variable-stiffness joints and compare how its hand antagonism and Floating Spring Joint achieve adjustability.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Read DLR's comparison:** list the positioning motors, stiffness-adjustment motors and spring arrangement for the hand and upper arm.
2. **Model two hypothetical linear presets:** at 0.1 radian twist, stiffnesses of 10 and 20 N·m/rad produce 1 and 2 N·m; real cam curves can be nonlinear.
3. **Make one worked distinction:** the documented Floating Spring Joint uses one large motor, one small motor and one spring; it is not two identical antagonistic drives.
4. **Watch the throwing demonstration:** identify where spring energy is stored and released; distinguish that sequence from merely increasing a position-control gain.

lessons.name: Bearings, structures and printed load paths
lessons.summary: Bearings guide motion while shafts, housings and fasteners carry loads into the robot frame; printed-part geometry and orientation affect that support.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Bearings guide motion while shafts, housings and fasteners carry loads into the robot frame; printed-part geometry and orientation affect that support.

![SKF cross-sections comparing contact angles and load directions in several rolling bearing types](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-bearings.webp)
*Bearing contact geometry determines which load directions it can support. Source: [SKF](https://www.skf.com/us/products/rolling-bearings/principles-of-rolling-bearing-selection/bearing-selection-process/bearing-type-and-arrangement/selection-criteria), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **The motor is not the whole joint:** force must pass from the moving link through its supports to the robot's base.
- **Loads have directions:** a bearing suited to sideways force is not automatically suitable for force along the shaft.
- **Printing adds another design decision:** Prusa explains that orientation and geometry affect the integrity of layer-by-layer printed parts.

> **Key idea:** Trace a continuous load path through every supporting part before increasing the motor's torque.

## How it works

- **Picture a shaft inside bearing rings:** rolling elements allow relative rotation while transmitting load between the shaft and housing.
- **Follow the reaction:** a loaded link pushes on the shaft; the bearing, housing and mounting connection must react to that force.
- **Think of an API dependency chain:** a robust service still fails if its downstream dependency fails; a strong motor still needs a suitable support structure.
- **Choose by load and geometry:** SKF distinguishes radial, axial and combined loads, and explains how contact angle changes axial load capability.
- **Check real assembly details:** ODRI's module instructions show bearings seated in shells and pulleys rather than floating in empty CAD space.
- **Prototype the fit:** Prusa warns there is no universal printed clearance; geometry, orientation, calibration and material all affect how parts fit together.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  L["Loaded link"] --> S["Shaft"]
  S --> B["Bearing"]
  B --> H["Printed housing"]
  H --> F["Fasteners and frame"]
```

## Key terms

- **Radial load**: force acting perpendicular to the shaft axis.
- **Axial load**: force acting along the shaft axis.
- **Housing**: the structure supporting a bearing's outer ring.
- **Contact angle**: the angle describing the load-transmitting contact direction inside a bearing.
- **Clearance**: deliberately allowed space between mating features.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Know basic forces and dimensions; use FreeCAD to identify shafts, bearing seats and the fixed frame in an assembly.
- **After:** Apply CAD and design for manufacture of robot joints, then Integrated legged and humanoid joint co-design.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Annotate an unpowered joint drawing:** trace one sideways load and one shaft-direction load all the way to the base.
2. **Use a sourced design allowance:** Prusa gives 0.3 mm as an initial clearance for movable printed parts, not a universal bearing-seat fit.
3. **Compare a hypothetical fit:** a 10.0 mm moving feature and 10.3 mm opening have 0.3 mm diametral clearance; actual fabrication still needs testing.
4. **Review print orientation:** rotate the proposed housing in CAD and list which features and load directions change relative to its layers.

lessons.name: CAD and design for manufacture of robot joints
lessons.summary: Robot-joint CAD describes geometry and allowed movement, while design for manufacture makes that model buildable, assemblable and adjustable in the real world.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Robot-joint CAD describes geometry and allowed movement, while design for manufacture makes that model buildable, assemblable and adjustable in the real world.

![Onshape robot assembly screenshot marking the top-level assembly, links and joint naming conventions](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-cad.webp)
*A robot assembly needs explicit links and joint conventions, not just attractive surfaces. Source: [onshape-to-robot](https://onshape-to-robot.readthedocs.io/en/latest/design.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A mesh is not a mechanism:** a printable shape does not by itself specify which parts move together or where the rotation axis lies.
- **Changes should propagate:** a parameter-driven model makes repeated dimensional changes easier than redrawing each related feature.
- **Fabrication has constraints:** Prusa documents overhangs, thin walls, orientation and clearance as design decisions, not cosmetic finishing details.

> **Key idea:** Treat the CAD assembly as an executable design specification, then test the assumptions fabrication cannot guarantee.

## How it works

- **Define geometry:** sketches and dimensions describe a part; an assembly combines those parts and specifies their connections.
- **Think of a build system:** shared parameters are inputs, features are dependent build steps, and an export is an artifact rather than the editable source.
- **Constrain movement explicitly:** a revolute connection allows rotation, while a fixed connection makes two components move together.
- **Plan the physical process:** examine whether the chosen printing orientation needs supports and whether mating parts have deliberate clearance.
- **Name robot joints for export:** onshape-to-robot interprets a revolute mate named `dof_elbow` as a robot joint named `elbow`.
- **Keep tool conventions separate:** that naming rule belongs to onshape-to-robot; it is not a universal rule imposed on every CAD application.
- **Handle loops deliberately:** a closed linkage needs additional closing constraints, not just a tree-shaped robot description.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Dimensions"] --> G["Part geometry"]
  G --> A["Assembly joints"]
  A --> M["Manufacturing review"]
  M --> T["Fit test"]
  T --> P
```

## Key terms

- **CAD**: computer-aided design, used to describe and inspect geometry.
- **Parameter**: an editable value that drives dimensions or feature choices.
- **Assembly**: connected components with specified relative positions and movement.
- **Mate**: a CAD relationship constraining how components connect.
- **Clearance**: intentional space that lets real manufactured components fit or move.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Read Bearings, structures and printed load paths and identify the moving shaft, supporting bearings and fixed housing.
- **After:** Use Linkages, cams and parallel mechanism design and Integrated legged and humanoid joint co-design to design complete moving assemblies.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Build a minimal hinge assembly:** model a fixed bracket and moving bar, then give their connection one rotational degree of freedom.
2. **Change a shared dimension:** verify that dependent geometry updates; keep the editable CAD file as well as the exported mesh.
3. **Work through the exporter example:** rename a hypothetical revolute mate `dof_elbow`; predict the exported joint name `elbow` and check the documented axis convention.
4. **Review manufacturability:** identify supports, mating clearance and assembly access; write down which dimensions need a test piece rather than assuming perfect printing.

lessons.name: Hydraulic and pneumatic transmission mechanics
lessons.summary: Hydraulic and pneumatic systems transmit power through pressurized liquid or gas, then turn pressure and flow into motion at an actuator.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Hydraulic and pneumatic systems transmit power through pressurized liquid or gas, then turn pressure and flow into motion at an actuator.

![Hydraulic cylinders and their connecting hoses mounted on an excavator arm](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-fluid-power.webp)
*Cylinders, hoses and the supply system form one power-transmission chain. Source: [National Fluid Power Association](https://www.nfpa.com/what-is-fluid-power-0/14333467044), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Linear motion comes naturally:** a cylinder moves a piston directly rather than requiring a rotating motor and screw.
- **The supply is part of the robot:** pumps or compressors, valves and hoses matter alongside the moving actuator.
- **Fluid actuation includes muscles:** Festo's DMSP contracts when pressurized, unlike a rigid cylinder with a sliding piston.

> **Key idea:** Pressure determines available effort, while displaced fluid and flow determine movement; neither quantity alone describes the system.

## How it works

- **Picture two connected syringes:** pushing one plunger moves liquid into the other; the National Fluid Power Association uses this example to explain hydraulic transmission.
- **Change the piston area:** a larger receiving piston can support more force at the same pressure, but moves less distance for the same displaced volume.
- **Follow a valve:** it routes fluid toward an actuator chamber or away from it, changing the movement direction.
- **Think of network traffic:** pressure resembles a driving difference and flow resembles throughput; a command still needs a complete transport path.
- **Distinguish the fluids:** hydraulics commonly uses oil; pneumatics commonly uses compressed air and has more cushioning because the gas compresses.
- **Compare a pneumatic muscle:** Festo describes flexible tubing reinforced with diamond-pattern fibres, which contracts under pressure and pulls in one direction.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Pump or compressor"] --> V["Valve"]
  V --> H["Hose and chamber"]
  H --> A["Piston or muscle"]
  A --> L["Mechanical load"]
```

## Key terms

- **Pressure**: force distributed over an area.
- **Flow rate**: fluid volume passing a point per unit time.
- **Piston**: a moving surface inside a cylinder that separates chambers and receives fluid force.
- **Double-acting cylinder**: a cylinder driven by pressure on either side of its piston.
- **Compressibility**: how much a material's volume changes under pressure.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Read Actuator sizing: torque, inertia and thermal duty; identify the load, required motion and complete operating cycle.
- **After:** Explore Soft pneumatic actuators and compliant-body fabrication and Tendon routing, antagonism and underactuated mechanisms.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Reproduce NFPA's syringe calculation:** a 1 square-inch piston supporting 10 pounds-force needs 10 psi of pressure to balance that load.
2. **Double the receiving diameter:** the area becomes four times larger; balancing the same load needs 2.5 psi, with one-quarter the travel per input stroke.
3. **Sketch the complete system:** include the pressure source, valve, hoses, actuator and return or exhaust path.
4. **Compare the robot paper:** identify why its authors combine remote tendons with pneumatic muscles rather than mounting motors directly in each moving joint.

> **Watch out:** Keep this exercise on paper; stored pressure can move an actuator unexpectedly even after an electrical command stops.

lessons.name: Soft pneumatic actuators and compliant-body fabrication
lessons.summary: Soft pneumatic actuators turn chamber inflation into bending or extension by combining elastic walls, carefully chosen geometry and constraints on stretching.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Soft pneumatic actuators turn chamber inflation into bending or extension by combining elastic walls, carefully chosen geometry and constraints on stretching.

![Soft Robotics Toolkit exploded diagram showing a row of PneuNet chambers above elastomer layers and an embedded paper layer](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-soft-pneumatic.webp)
*The chambered body bends above a paper-reinforced, strain-limiting base. Source: [Soft Robotics Toolkit](https://softroboticstoolkit.com/book/pneunets-design), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **The body is the mechanism:** wall thickness and material behaviour replace much of the rigid linkage and gearbox design.
- **A gripping shape can emerge from inflation:** Harvard's PneuNet gripper video shows soft fingers bending around an object.
- **Fabrication affects behaviour:** a convincing CAD shape is not enough; the chambers and bonded base must form a usable sealed actuator.

> **Key idea:** Design the constraint on expansion, not just the empty space that holds air.

## How it works

- **Picture connected air chambers:** the PneuNets design places them in a row inside an elastic material, with thin walls between neighbouring chambers.
- **Inflate unevenly:** thin, compliant regions expand more readily than regions that resist stretching.
- **Restrict the base:** the documented design embeds paper in an elastomer base; this strain-limiting layer prevents equal lengthening on both sides.
- **Produce bending:** the expanding chamber side grows longer than the restricted base, curving the actuator rather than simply stretching it straight.
- **Think of configuration-driven software:** changing the chamber layout or material changes the response to the same pressure input, even with identical control code.
- **Cast and bond:** the toolkit molds the main body and base separately, then uses uncured elastomer to join them.
- **Measure the result:** the testing guide records tip trajectories and separately measures delivered force; those are different performance questions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Air pressure"] --> C["Chamber expansion"]
  C --> D["Unequal stretching"]
  D --> B["Bending"]
  B --> T["Tip and force tests"]
```

## Key terms

- **Elastomer**: a rubber-like material capable of substantial elastic deformation.
- **PneuNet**: a pneumatic network of connected chambers that deforms when pressurized.
- **Strain**: change in length relative to the starting length.
- **Strain-limiting layer**: a layer that restricts stretching on one side of the actuator.
- **Curing**: the process by which the cast material sets into its usable solid form.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Study Hydraulic and pneumatic transmission mechanics and CAD and design for manufacture of robot joints.
- **After:** Explore PneuNet chamber geometry sketch study, Soft actuator mold and seal coupon kit and Artificial muscles: electrohydraulic and smart-material actuation.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Trace the documented cross-section:** label one chamber, the thin wall beside it and the paper-reinforced base.
2. **Compare two paper designs:** keep chamber height fixed in one; make the separating walls thinner in the other and predict the easier-expanding region.
3. **Replicate the test plan:** the toolkit records three inflation–deflation cycles to estimate a tip trajectory; specify how you would compare those three traces.
4. **Write fabrication checkpoints:** separate mold preparation, casting, bonding and curing; use the published testing method to define what a successful specimen must demonstrate.

lessons.name: Artificial muscles: electrohydraulic and smart-material actuation
lessons.summary: Artificial muscles create motion through deforming materials or fluid-filled structures, with different electrical, thermal and mechanical requirements from conventional rotary motors.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Artificial muscles create motion through deforming materials or fluid-filled structures, with different electrical, thermal and mechanical requirements from conventional rotary motors.

![ETH Zurich diagram showing the layered HALVE artificial muscle and its oil-filled pouch](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-artificial-muscles.webp)
*HALVE separates the load-bearing shell, electrode and electrical-insulation layers. Source: [ETH Zurich Soft Robotics Lab](https://srl.ethz.ch/platforms/ems/halve.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A joint need not start with rotation:** an actuator can contract, bend or fold directly, then connect to a larger mechanism.
- **Actuator families are not interchangeable:** an electrohydraulic pouch and a heat-driven shape-memory element need different models and driving hardware.
- **Published context matters:** HALVE's reduced voltage is relative to earlier electrohydraulic muscles, not an ordinary low-voltage electronics interface.

> **Key idea:** Compare complete force, motion and energy-conversion mechanisms, not the shared label “artificial muscle.”

## How it works

- **Picture HALVE's layered pouch:** it contains oil, electrodes and an insulating material designed to store electrical energy.
- **Apply electrical attraction:** opposite electrodes draw together, displacing the oil into the remaining pouch volume and changing the actuator's shape.
- **Separate material roles:** ETH's design uses a structural shell for mechanical support and a high-permittivity layer for the electrical function.
- **Think of hardware backends:** two implementations may expose a similar “contract” operation while needing completely different power sources and state models.
- **Compare shape-memory actuation:** the 2025 microactuator paper uses temperature-driven bending of a shape-memory-alloy film combined with magnetic latching.
- **Keep measurement conditions attached:** ETH reports HALVE operation at 1100 V; that number describes a particular research design, not every artificial muscle.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  E["Electrical input"] --> A["Electrode attraction"]
  A --> F["Oil displacement"]
  F --> C["Pouch contraction"]
  C --> L["Load movement"]
```

## Key terms

- **Electrohydraulic**: combining an electrical effect with fluid movement to create mechanical motion.
- **Dielectric**: an electrically insulating material used between conductive regions.
- **Permittivity**: a property describing how a material responds to an electric field.
- **Stroke**: the useful travel or change in length of an actuator.
- **Shape-memory alloy**: a metal whose temperature-dependent material behaviour can produce a designed shape change.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Study Soft pneumatic actuators and compliant-body fabrication; distinguish deformation of a chamber from rotation of a rigid joint.
- **After:** Build Artificial muscle force-stroke evidence atlas before Electrohydraulic pouch mechanics model or Thermal magnetic folding mechanism digital twin.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Build an evidence table:** compare HALVE with the shape-memory microactuator using input energy, moving material, output motion and reset mechanism.
2. **Work one reported comparison:** 1100 V is 1.1 kV; label it as HALVE's published driving voltage rather than interpreting “low-voltage” as hobby-safe.
3. **Trace the gripper video:** identify the deforming muscles, mechanical connection and lifted object; separate the actuator from its power supply.
4. **Mark missing quantities unknown:** do not rank force or efficiency unless both sources report comparable loads, strokes and measurement conditions.

> **Watch out:** Keep this exercise digital; 1100 V still requires specialist high-voltage engineering and is not a beginner breadboard experiment.

lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Joint co-design chooses the actuator, transmission, structure and packaging together so a leg or humanoid can deliver the intended motion as a complete machine.

![ToddlerBot mechatronic design figure showing joint locations, body structure and integrated electronics](/img/lessons/knowledge_mechanisms_actuation-joint-co-design.webp)
*ToddlerBot documents active joints alongside the sensors, electronics and body they must fit. Source: [ToddlerBot project](https://toddlerbot.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A good motor can make a poor leg:** it still needs supports, a usable range of motion and a transmission that fits the body.
- **Repeated units need integration details:** ODRI reuses actuator cores across different structures rather than treating every joint as an unrelated mechanism.
- **Assembly and maintenance are design inputs:** ToddlerBot publishes assembly resources alongside its learning and control software.

> **Key idea:** Evaluate a candidate inside its complete joint envelope and task, not as an isolated catalogue component.

## How it works

- **Start from motion and load:** identify what the foot or hand must do before deciding where motors and supporting structures belong.
- **Inspect a concrete leg:** ODRI's three-degree-of-freedom leg uses three actuator cores in hip and leg subassemblies.
- **Follow packaging consequences:** its documentation includes an alternative hip shell specifically to simplify wire routing.
- **Check travel limits:** the same leg documents optional mechanical stops to prevent repeated rotations from winding up wires.
- **Think of full-stack performance:** optimizing one function cannot fix a bottleneck in another layer; motor, transmission, structure and control share a system budget.
- **Compare complete platforms:** ToddlerBot's published design shows 30 active degrees of freedom, with six per leg, rather than only a standalone servo.
- **Keep validation separate:** a model that fits together still needs load, motion and repeated-operation tests; a rendered walking pose is not endurance evidence.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T["Task and motion"] --> A["Actuator and ratio"]
  A --> S["Supports and structure"]
  S --> P["Cables and packaging"]
  P --> V["System tests"]
  V --> T
```

## Key terms

- **Co-design**: choosing interacting subsystems together rather than independently.
- **Joint envelope**: the space available for a joint and its moving components.
- **Actuator core**: reusable internal components that can be integrated into different surrounding structures.
- **Range of motion**: the joint positions mechanically available without collision or exceeding travel limits.
- **Distal mass**: mass farther along a limb, away from the robot's body.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Study Actuator sizing: torque, inertia and thermal duty, Bearings, structures and printed load paths and Backdrivability, friction and mechanical transparency.
- **After:** Try Humanoid knee packaging teardown in CAD, then Equal-envelope leg joint Pareto study before Captive single-leg actuator test stand.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Read ODRI's component table:** identify three repeated cores and separate them from hip shells, upper leg and lower leg parts.
2. **Work a documented mass subtotal:** three 95 g cores total 285 g; the listed complete leg is 485 g, leaving 200 g for everything else.
3. **List packaging checks:** include bearing support, wire routing, joint stops and assembly sequence for one hypothetical joint replacement.
4. **Compare with ToddlerBot:** use its leg assembly and design figure to explain why a six-joint humanoid leg is more than six unrelated motor selections.
